title: A Message Delivered
subtitle: We live in independence, yet we depend on others to survive.

trails.title: Unofficial Map
trails.description: The nameless black dots on this parchment cry out for annotations.

content.text: Excerpt from "A History of Arcane Ethnicity"

...

Due to the reclusive nature of the Nukutais, our knowledge of this enigmatic people comes only from the sparse accounts of a few trading ships that had contact with them and the legends from neighboring societies.

...

In the folklore of coastal civilizations in the South Pacific, there are often tales of Shell People or Hermit Crab People. These beings, dressed in shells and living in the water, are depicted as otherworldly ocean emissaries or guardians. They offer advice and guidance to the protagonists in these stories or help those lost at sea.

...

With the Age of Exploration, the veil over these mysterious figures was lifted, and a small island named Nukutaeao, known for its production of mystical and esoteric crafts, became a topic of intrigue among adventurers in taverns. Consequently, the intrusion of explorers and trading ships seemed to weary the Nukutais, and records from that period show they gradually vanished from the pages of history. They employed some form of arcane skill to conceal the island's exact location, ensuring their homeland never appeared on any official map.

...

Today, with advancements in maritime technology and increasing global communication, it is only a matter of time before the island of the Nukutais is rediscovered. The author can only hope that this inevitable encounter will not bring undue harm to the Nukutais, wishing that they can integrate into the global community through peaceful and friendly exchanges. May the final chapter of this Age of Exploration conclude with harmony.

items.text: When the first proverb appears on the shell, we reach the shores of elsewhere—the island, the upturned palm of Mother Sea.
The once drifting boat now beds itself in the golden sand.
When the second proverb appears on the shell, we kindle the fire—the crackling warmth, the spark of hope.
The joyful people are long blessed as one.
When the third proverb appears on the shell, we accept the sea's gift—the rolling waves, the plentiful fish.
The cool sea breeze cradles us.
When the fourth proverb appears on the shell, we face the test—the salty tears, the longing gaze.
Beyond the sea, I find no home.
Beach, Nukutaeao

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: You did well today, Tutu.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Thank you, Kamuta! I was just playing my part in celebrating the success of the trade season. Nothing special, really.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: But what are we doing here? What could be more important than the celebration?

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: I've never seen you sneak off on a bonfire night before.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Tutu, do you think you and your friends could fix up that old ship?

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: I know you're close with Toa, Selone, and the rest. They always make sure their first fous go to you. I'm sure they'd be happy to lend you a hand.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: And the elders like you, too. I've heard many of them say they'll leave their Spirit Shells to you. So you can win their support, too, right?

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Woah! Slow down, big chief! Are you saying you want to fix up the Quick Spear?

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Hm! Yeah.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: But why? We've kept it docked for years.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Maybe one day we'll need to set sail again—to fish or spend some time on another island.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: But, the merchants already come by every few months to bring us hala fruits and red snappers. Why would we need to sail?
Kamuta paces back and forth in front of Fatutu, the words stuck in his throat.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Yeah, but what if a storm hits? Are we just going to sit around and let the waves wash away our homes?

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: We've been through much worse than a few storms.
She raises her head proudly.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Remember when the waves came and took away Malaga? Heilani cried for days over that little pebble castle.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: And then that strange oil polluted the water all around Itiiti—the only place where the water's calm enough to hold the Paopao race. We haven't held a race since.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Then Miti and Vaipuna ...

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: But we've made it through, because that's what we do in the face of difficulties, right? We stick together. Besides, we're doing just fine on Meli.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: But what if we lose Meli to the waves as well?

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: If it comes to that, Tutu, I need you to take everyone and leave—find somewhere to stay for a while. Can I ask that of you?
Fatutu's brow furrows.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: You've been acting strange, brother. Are you thinking of sneaking off and leaving us?

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: I'm not going anywhere. I promise.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Neither are the rest of us, brother.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: No! You must get ready. Start preparing now!
Kamuta's unusual behavior leads Fatutu to make a bold guess.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Something's been bothering you since last trade season. You've been spending a lot of time on the beach, looking out to the sea.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Did a witch put a spell on you?

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: You better wear some molukka around your neck and carry knitbones and dulse leaves.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: No, no, there's no witch. It's just something Ms. Grace told me. It's been bugging me.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Ms. Grace? That outsider who calls herself a captain?
With the singing of the Nukutai, the trade festival slowly comes to an end.
On the beach, the Nukutai bid farewell to their guests in twos and threes, enjoying this rare moment of leisure.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: I don't mean to alarm you, Mr. Kamuta.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: But three months from now, Meli will be devoured by a tsunami.
She stands nonchalantly, as if discussing something insignificant.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Ms. Grace, don't say such nonsense!

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: You're welcome as a guest, but that doesn't give you the right to spread fear among my people.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: What if I told you that the sinking of Malaga and Vaipuna wasn't entirely caused by the tsunami, but there were other factors at play?

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: It is true that the tsunami sent them into the sea. But long before it struck, foreign military forces had been eyeing the islands for their strategic value.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Those rumbling sounds ... They weren't thunder?!

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: They were torpedoes launched by humans.
She presents a thick document in her hand.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: And I have some unfortunate news regarding them.
Kamuta grabs the cold, impersonal stack of white paper.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: "The area is now under martial law. Any development plans for the region should be revised accordingly."

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: These coordinates ... they cover Nukutaeao.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: After a brief investigation, they concluded that your home is an unoccupied area suitable for their weapon testing.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: It won't be long before they publish a report on this new test site and receive their rewards for discovering it.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: The Veil of Nothingness was cast by our ancestors to protect us from the outside world.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: I never thought it would put us at risk.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: As Chief, I must bring this to the attention of my people. Perhaps it's time we removed the mist. But without it, we'll draw all kinds of attention.
Kamuta clenches the report tightly in his fist.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Ms. Grace, may I borrow this document? My people need to see this.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: Be my guest. But you'd better persuade them quickly.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Why's that?

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: As far as I know, they're looking to expand the test site. It's on their agenda now.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Right. We'll have to set up a meeting with them to negotiate.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: Certainly. I wish you the best of luck persuading those warmongers, and for your safety in the coming tsunami.
Every nonchalant word that leaves her mouth strikes Kamuta with the shocking gravity of the situation.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: With all due respect, Ms. Grace ...

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Not even the Nukutai can predict the movements of the ocean that far in advance. On what basis are you making this forecast?

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: It's not a forecast, Mr. Kamuta.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: Call it the wisdom of hindsight.

items.speaker: Ms. Grace
items.text: Or perhaps, I should put it more clearly. Have you heard of the "Storm"?

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Kamuta! Kamuta! Brother!

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: The rain's getting heavier! We must go inside!
Rain blurs Kamuta's vision.
He stares into the distance, his eyes widening as the frothing waves roar toward the coast. The sea level is rising.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: It's the tsunami. It's happening.
Like the soil beneath the ever-rising waterline, Kamuta's murmured words are quickly buried.
The sea has almost swallowed the whole atoll.

items.speaker: Toa
items.text: What's going on, Tutu? Kamuta?
A worried figure hurries over.

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: No time for questions, Toa! We must bring these baskets to safety!
Fatutu is already pushing as many woven baskets filled with berries and bundled material as she can up to higher ground. Her hands are a sore red, her face stamped with desperate determination.

items.speaker: Toa
items.text: Ah, there's food and clothes in there!

items.speaker: Selone
items.text: Here, I'll give you a hand!
A tall figure rushes over, grabbing the baskets from the children's hands and tossing them aside.

items.speaker: Selone
items.text: Chief, what are you doing?!

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Leave them! There's no time! We must get to the ship! Now!

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: Our people still have to live after the flood's over!

items.speaker: Fatutu
items.text: If we don't bring something, what are we going to eat or wear? These things won't fall into our laps, you know.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Listen! It's different this time. You—
Before Kamuta can finish speaking, a few dark shadows dart out from the forest.
*roar*

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: Tutu! Watch out!
A row of sharp claws grazes Kamuta's back.

items.speaker: Toa
items.text: What are all these Splintercats doing here?!

items.speaker: Selone
items.text: The near-endless surge of critters starts to create an even greater panic.

items.speaker: Selone
items.text: These aren't just Splintercats! Are those Sarmatian Sea Snails? And crabs with ghost faces?!

items.speaker: Toa
items.text: I've never seen them all come out together before. What kind of storm is this?!
In the flashes of lightning, doubt and worry flicker across the Nukutai's faces.

items.speaker: Kamuta
items.text: They can sense the coming tsunami! Come, we need more hands to drive them off!

items.speaker: Toa
items.text: Understood!
